props.title: A Company Man

sections.content: **A Company Man (2012)** (2012) exemplifies the sleek, brutal efficiency of modern Korean action cinema. Like I Saw the Devil (2010) and The Man from Nowhere (2010), it wraps corporate critique in stylized violence. The film follows Hyeong-do, a hitman whose murder corporation operates under the facade of a metal manufacturing company - a brilliant metaphor for how corporate culture dehumanizes workers. This builds on themes from **Office** (2015) and **Falling Down** (1993), but with the distinctly Korean approach to action choreography that influenced films like **John Wick** (2014).

sections.content: The film's commentary on toxic work culture resonates with other Korean corporate thrillers like Veteran (2015) and Inside Men (2015). Director Lim Sang-yoon crafts action sequences with mechanical precision - conference rooms transform into killing floors, briefcases conceal weapons, and corporate attire becomes combat gear. The sterile office environments mirror similar settings in **Office Space** (1999) and **Mayhem** (2017), but with a darker, more lethal edge.

So Ji-sub's performance as Hyeong-do channels the contained intensity of **Leon: The Professional** (1994) while adding distinctly Korean corporate elements. The film's exploration of work-life balance through extreme violence predates similar themes in **Severance** (2022) and **Sorry to Bother You** (2018), showing how Korean cinema often leads in mixing genre elements with social commentary. sections.content: The film's action choreography deserves special attention, building on the foundation laid by **The Raid** (2011) and **Oldboy** (2003). Each fight scene emphasizes efficiency over spectacle - much like the corporate world it satirizes. The precision of violence mirrors similar approaches in **The Villainess** (2017) and **New World** (2013), where professional killers operate within rigid organizational structures.
